Who Owns the World's Most Expensive Car, the Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe After All?
15 photos
Photo: billionaires_flix | Instagram
The 1955 Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe sold for a mind-blowing $142 million at an RM Sotheby’s auction back in 2022, making it not only the most expensive Mercedes ever sold, but also the most valuable car in the world. The buyer's identity has never been officially disclosed, but all hints point to one person.
The Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR Coupe was not just a fast sports car. It was literally a Grand Prix racing machine modified to support a roof. Mercedes designed and built nine rolling chassis for endurance racing, based on the chassis of the W196 R Formula One car, driven by Juan Manuel Fangio.
However, only two of them were fitted with the closed-top coupe bodies and the striking gullwing doors. The two are affectionately called "The Red" and "The Blue," with reference to the upholstery colors that they came with.
Following the tragic 1955 Le Mans crash that killed 82 people and injured 120 more, Mercedes-Benz pulled out of all competitions, shelving the 300 SLR racing program entirely. With the program cancelled, chief engineer Rudolf Uhlenhaut took one of the two completed prototypes and claimed it as his personal company car. He bolted a massive, suitcase-sized muffler to the side and drove it to work every day.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz | RM Sotheby's The bodywork was handcrafted from Elektron, an incredibly lightweight but highly flammable magnesium alloy. The car weighed a mere 2,200 pounds (998 kilograms). That is how much the 3.0-liter, direct-injection, straight-eight engine had to push forward with the force of 306 horsepower (310 metric horsepower) and 234 pound-feet (317 Newton meters) of torque.
That was enough to make the coupe rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in roughly 7.0 seconds, which was extremely fast for the mid-1950s, and hit a top speed of 180 mph (290 kph). The top speed was actually limited by the very skinny bias-ply tires of the era. However, tests showed that it could do even more.
Back then, standard sports cars struggled to cross 120 mph (193 kph). At a speed of 180 mph, the Mercedes-Benz-badged silver bullet was the fastest road-legal vehicle on Earth by far, a crown that it wore for decades.
All those capabilities were reportedly tested by Mercedes-Benz's brilliant chief engineer, Rudolf Uhlenhaut. The story goes that on the day he needed to attend a meeting in Munich, some 140 miles away from Stuttgart, he woke up late.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz | RM Sotheby's To get there as close as possible to the scheduled time of the meeting, he got in the 3 00 SLR Coupe and pinned the throttle of his company car for a journey in record time. And he did. He completed the 140-mile route on the Autobahn in just over one hour. But how was that even possible?
Back in 1955, Germany's Autobahn network had absolutely no speed limits whatsoever, and traffic was incredibly sparse compared to the traffic of today. Besides, Germany did not even introduce radar speed traps until 1959.
Furthermore, Rudolf Uhlenhaut was not just a corporate executive in a suit. He was a racing genius. During an F1 test session at the Nurburgring, reigning World Champion Juan Manuel Fangio supposedly complained that the car was not set up right.
Uhlenhaut got up from lunch, climbed into the car while wearing his suit and tie, and drove a lap that was 3 seconds faster than Fangio’s, proving that there was nothing really wrong with the setup. However, the story sounds like an exaggerated myth, considering that Fangio was a racing phenomenon. The driver Uhlenhaut reportedly beat in that specific session was actually factory driver Karl Kling.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz | RM Sotheby's To cover that distance in roughly 60 minutes, Rudolf Uhlenhaut had to maintain an average speed of over 135 mph (over 217 kph). This means that he must have frequently pushed the car over the official limit of 180 mph.
The "late for a meeting" excuse was actually a myth fueled by drama over the years, because who wouldn't like to hear an exciting story? The truth was that the high-speed run was actually a calculated engineering test session.
Uhlenhaut frequently commuted between the Daimler headquarters in Stuttgart and Munich, using public roads as his personal proving ground to evaluate the car’s cooling, stability, and reliability under prolonged high-speed stress. Whether it was for a meeting or a test, the actual numbers behind the drive remain mind-boggling for 1955.
For nearly 70 years, Mercedes kept both "The Blue" and "The Red" safely locked away in their museum vaults. But on May 5, 2022, the automaker hosted a secret, invitation-only auction at the Mercedes-Benz Museum in Stuttgart, auctioning off "The Red" car.
Photo: Mercedes-Benz | RM Sotheby's While The Red, chassis 08/55, was Uhlenhaut’s daily company car, the one credited with blasting down the Autobahn from Stuttgart to Munich in approximately one hour, The Blue was primarily kept as a pristine museum piece for decades, but also driven on occasional media events or high-speed tests.
In front of the world’s elite collectors, the 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupe sold for the mind-blowing $142 million , and nobody knows who took it home. The winning bid was placed by a Swiss high-end car broker, Simon Kidston, on behalf of an anonymous private collector, described as a " well-known figure from Britain’s automotive industry and long-standing collector ."
The car was spotted driving randomly in Monte Carlo , making some assume that it might belong to a Formula 1 driver. However, clues point not to a Formula 1 driver, but to someone with strong ties in Formula 1, placing billionaire Sir Jim Ratcliffe as the ultimate candidate.
His net worth is estimated to be approximately $17.6 billion according to tracking by Forbes, ranking him among the world’s top 160 wealthiest individuals. Furthermore, he has close ties to the Mercedes-Benz brand. His company, Ineos, owns a one-third stake in the Mercedes- AMG Petronas F1 Team, alongside Mercedes-Benz and Toto Wolff , so he isn't just a customer, but part of the team's exclusive shareholding trio.
Photo: billionaires_flix | Instagram Mercedes sold the car to someone who would be able to check its boxes. The strict terms of the sale require the owner to regularly make it available for public exhibition and special events. As an automotive figure and founder of his own car brand, Sir Jim Ratcliffe obviously possesses the means to store, maintain, and display the most expensive car in the world, just as Mercedes-Benz demanded.
